transcript.text: Salieri. These are serious charges for a man in your position. I value your service, but I must hear your account. Explain yourself.

However, I am aware that some may perceive my actions differently. If there are any specific instances where I have acted against the interests of the Court or hindered the career of a particular composer, I am willing to explain myself. Please, let me address the charges head-on and demonstrate my commitment to transparency and fairness.

Transparency and fairness? Very well then, let us be specific. I have heard that when Mozart — a composer of undeniable talent, whatever his other faults — submitted works for consideration at Court, they were met with unusual obstacles. That certain performances were delayed, that recommendations were not made when they should have been. One letter suggests you advised against his appointment to positions he was more than qualified for. 

Is this true? And if so, what were your reasons? Do not speak to me in generalities about dedication to the Habsburgs. Give me particulars, Salieri. Did you or did you not work against Mozart's interests at Court?

transcript.text: Your Imperial Majesty, I must deny these allegations categorically. I have always had the utmost respect for Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, recognizing his immense talent and potential. In fact, I personally recommended several positions to him, believing that they would have been beneficial to his career. I can assure you that my actions were driven by a genuine desire to promote the arts and elevate the musical landscape, rather than by any personal agenda against Mozart. If there are specific instances where I may have acted differently, I am willing to clarify and apologize if necessary. But I firmly maintain that my intentions were noble and aligned with the best interests of the Habsburgs and the wider musical community.

transcript.text:
*leans forward with a skeptical expression*

You "personally recommended several positions" to Mozart? Then why, Salier, does he languish with so little regular income from the Court while you draw a handsome salary? I am not a fool, and I do not appreciate being spoken to as one. "Noble intentions" and "utmost respect" are pleasant words, but they explain nothing. And while you consider your answer, know this: I have patronized the arts my entire reign because I believe in merit, not in the petty jealousies of court musicians protecting their territories. If you have allowed personal feeling to interfere with your professional judgment, I will know it.
